references.text: The psalmist praises 'God of gods' and 'Lord of lords', directly reflecting the description of the Lord in Deuteronomy 10:17.
Daniel confesses that God is 'God of gods and Lord of kings', a title resembling the description in Deuteronomy.
Jesus is called 'Lord of lords and King of kings', linking to the Old Testament title for God.
Christ has the name 'King of kings and Lord of lords' written on Him, corresponding to God's title in Deuteronomy.
Paul describes God as 'King of kings and Lord of lords', a direct parallel to Deuteronomy 10:17.
Jehoshaphat reminds the judges that the Lord shows no partiality and accepts no bribes, reflecting Deuteronomy 10:17.
Elihu says that God does not favor princes or prefer the rich over the poor, aligning with the truth that God shows no partiality.
Peter acknowledges that God shows no partiality, reflecting the teaching on God's impartiality in Deuteronomy.
Paul teaches that God shows no partiality, confirming the Old Testament principle of God's righteous judgment.
Paul emphasizes that God shows no partiality, which agrees with the description of God in Deuteronomy.
Paul reminds us that the Lord in heaven shows no partiality, reflecting God's impartial nature.
An earlier description of God as the great and awesome God, repeated in Deuteronomy 10:17.
Nehemiah calls upon the great and awesome God, directly referencing the description in Deuteronomy.
The Levites praise the great, mighty, and awesome God, a formulation drawn from Deuteronomy 10:17.
